Here is a conservative 3-week reconditioning block designed to reintroduce load safely and bring the client back toward pre-illness baselines. It emphasizes low-to-moderate volume, gradual frequency ramp, and close attention to fatigue, heart rate, and recovery. You can adjust based on daily readiness, but aim to complete each week with the prescribed structure and only progress when criteria are met (see progression notes).

Overview and goals
- Goals: reintroduce movement patterns, rebuild confidence and tolerance, restore baseline strength curves, minimize relapse/overreach, monitor appetite and energy.
- Weekly structure: 4 training days per week (2 lower-body focused days, 2 upper-body focused days), with a light conditioning/recovery touch on day 7 (optional). All lifts performed with controlled tempo, no ballistic movements, and RPE targets.
- Progression principle: start near 60–70% of pre-illness loads for the first week, increase to ~70–80% by Week 2, and approach 80–90% of baseline by Week 3 only if readiness metrics allow. Use RPE 6–7 early, moving to RPE 7–8 by Week 3 for main compound lifts.
- Indicators of readiness: resting heart rate, appetite, sleep quality, no excessive soreness, stable mood, no fever or persistent fatigue (>48 hours). If symptoms return or fatigue spikes, scale back.

Baseline estimates (for reference)
- Pre-illness max estimates: Bench 100 kg, Squat 140 kg, Deadlift 170 kg.
- Repetition targets will be conservative; assume 1RM guidance: bench ~95–105% of current ability in the plan only after reconditioning; use rating of perceived exertion (RPE) and velocity where available.

Week-by-week plan (3 weeks total)

 Week 1: Reintroduction and capacity restoration
- Training days: 4 days (e.g., Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat)
- Daily structure: 60–75 minutes; emphasis on stability, movement quality, and gradual load.

Day A – Upper body (bench emphasis)
- Warm-up: 5–10 minutes light cardio + dynamic shoulder/thoracic mobility
- floor press or bench press (main lift): 3 sets x 6 reps @ RPE 6 (submax)
- Dumbbell or barbell incline press: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6
- Seated cable row or Pendlay row: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Dumbbell shoulder press (neutral grip): 3 x 10 @ RPE 6–7
- Lat pull-down or pull-up progressions: 3 x 8–10 @ RPE 6–7
- Accessory core: 2 x 12-15 (anti-rotational or hollow holds)
- Conditioning (optional): 10 minutes light aerobic work or mobility work

Day B – Lower body (squat/deadlift emphasis, lighter volume)
- Warm-up: 5–10 minutes cardio + ankle/hip mobility
- Back squat (or goblet if needed): 3 x 5 @ RPE 6
- Romanian deadlift or stiff-leg deadlift: 3 x 6 @ RPE 6–7
- Leg press or belt squats: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Split squats or bulgarian split squats: 3 x 8 per leg @ RPE 6–7
- Calf raises: 3 x 12–15
- Core: 2 x 12 (plank variations)

Day C – Upper body (pulling emphasis and symmetry) – light
- Warm-up: 5–10 minutes
- Barbell or dumbbell bench row: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Seated cable row or inverted rows: 3 x 10 @ RPE 6–7
- Lat pulldown or assisted pull-ups: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Dumbbell lateral raises: 3 x 12 @ RPE 6–7
- Triceps pushdown or skull crushers: 3 x 10 @ RPE 6–7
- Grip/forearm work: 2 x 12–15
- Mobility/rotator cuff work: 5–10 minutes

Day D – Lower body accessory and conditioning
- Warm-up: 5–10 minutes
- Trap bar or barbell deadlift (light): 3 x 4–5 @ RPE 6
- Hip thrust or glute bridge: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Lunges or step-ups: 3 x 8 per leg @ RPE 6–7
- Glute/ham raise or hamstring curls: 3 x 10 @ RPE 6–7
- Core: 2 x 12
- Conditioning: 8–12 minutes easy pace (zone 2)

Weekly notes for Week 1
- Volume and intensity are deliberately low. Focus on form, bracing, and breathing. Keep rest periods 60–90 seconds on most sets; extend to 2 minutes on heavier lifts if needed.
- Monitor appetite and energy. If fatigue is high beyond expected, reduce two sets from one or two exercises or skip optional conditioning.
- Sleep target: 7–9 hours.

Week 2: Gradual load increase and single-sport emphasis
- Training days: 4 days (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat)
- Objective: nudge intensity up while maintaining technique and recovery. Slightly higher RPE targets (6–7 for most sets; 7–8 for some main lifts depending on readiness).

Day A – Upper body (bench emphasis) – moderate
- Warm-up: same
- Bench press or floor press: 4 x 5 @ RPE 6–7
- Overhead press: 3 x 6 @ RPE 6–7
- Barbell row: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Dumbbell incline press: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Pull-ups or lat pulldown: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Triceps/face pull work: 2 x 12-15
- Core: 2 x 12

Day B – Lower body (squat focus, volume up slightly)
- Warm-up
- Back squat: 4 x 4 @ RPE 6–7
- Romanian deadlift: 3 x 6 @ RPE 6–7
- Leg press or hack squat: 3 x 8 @ RPE 6–7
- Bulgarian split squat: 3 x 8 per leg @ RPE 6–7
- Calf raises: 3 x 12–15
- Core: 2 x 12

Day C – Upper body (pulling emphasis) – moderate
- Warm-up
- Barbell row or t-bar row: 4 x 6 @ RPE 6–7
- Pull-ups/assisted: 3 x 6–8 @ RPE 6–7
- Dumbbell or cable lateral raises: 3 x 10–12
- Chest-supported row: 3 x 8–10
- Face pulls: 3 x 12–15
- Biceps work: 2 x 10–12
- Mobility work: 5–10 minutes

Day D – Lower body accessory + conditioning
- Warm-up
- Trap bar deadlift or deadlift from blocks: 3 x 4–5 @ RPE 6
- Hip thrust: 3 x 6–8 @ RPE 6–7
- Front rack reverse lunges: 3 x 6 per leg @ RPE 6–7
- Hamstring curls: 3 x 10
- Core: 2 x 12
- Conditioning: 10–15 minutes easy, zone 2

Week 3: Return toward baseline strength and higher intensity
- Training days: 4 days (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat)
- Objective: approach baseline strength levels with higher quality reps. Expect RPEs around 7–8 on main lifts.

Day A – Upper body (bench emphasis) – near baseline
- Warm-up
- Bench press: 3 x 5 @ RPE 7–8 (aim for controlled, near-rep max)
- Incline dumbbell bench or press: 3 x 6–7 @ RPE 7
- Barbell row or chest-supported row: 3 x 6–8 @ RPE 7
- Overhead press: 3 x 6 @ RPE 7
- Lat pulldown: 3 x 8 @ RPE 7
- Core: 2 x 12
- Optional accessory finisher: 5–8 minutes diagonal cable rotations or anti-extension

Day B – Lower body (squat/deadlift emphasis) – near baseline
- Warm-up
- Back squat: 3 x 4–5 @ RPE 7–8
- Deadlift (conventional or sumo, light-to-moderate): 3 x 4–5 @ RPE 7–8
- Leg press or hack squat: 3 x 6–8 @ RPE 7
- Romanian deadlift: 3 x 6 @ RPE 7
- Calf raises: 3 x 12–15
- Core: 2 x 12

Day C – Upper body (pulling emphasis) – near baseline
- Warm-up
- Pull-ups/lat pulldown: 4 x 6–8 @ RPE 7
- Barbell row: 3 x 6–8 @ RPE 7
- Seated cable row: 3 x 8–10 @ RPE 7
- Dumbbell incline press or push-ups: 3 x 8–10 @ RPE 7
- Face pulls: 3 x 12–15
- Biceps work: 2 x 10–12
- Mobility and shoulder health: 7–10 minutes

Day D – Lower body accessory and conditioning
- Warm-up
- Front squat (light) or goblet squat: 3 x 5 @ RPE 7
- Hip thrust or glute bridge: 3 x 6–8 @ RPE 7
- Bulgarian split squat: 3 x 6 per leg @ RPE 7
- Hamstring curls: 3 x 8–10
- Core: 2 x 12
- Conditioning: 12–15 minutes moderate pace (bike or treadmill)

Notes on progression and safety
- If any symptoms return (fatigue, fever, chest tightness), pull back immediately: reduce sets by 20–30% or revert to Week 1 structure until symptoms subside.
- Use RPE rather than load progression alone to gauge progress. If you’re consistently below RPE 6 on key lifts for two sessions in a row, you can test small increases a week earlier, otherwise stay the course.
- Temperature and pulse: monitor resting heart rate each morning. An increase of >5–8 beats per minute over baseline on several days in a row can indicate insufficient recovery; consider backing off volume/intensity.
- All reps should be controlled with a 2–3 second eccentric and 1–2 seconds concentric phases unless otherwise noted. Breathing: exhale on the concentric portion, brace the core for compound movements.

Nutrition and recovery guidance
- Calorie intake: aim for maintenance or slight surplus to regain 4 kg weight; support recovery with protein intake around 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day (rough target 140–180 g/day for a 90–100 kg client; adjust to actual weight and needs).
- Protein timing: 20–40 g per meal; include protein with snacks.
- Carbohydrates: ensure adequate carbs around training to support performance and recovery; emphasize whole grains, fruits, vegetables.
- Fats: maintain healthy fats; don't drop to extremely low-fat diets.
- Hydration: 2.5–3.5 L/day depending on sweat rate and climate.
- Sleep: aim for 7–9 hours; consider a short 10–20 minute power nap if energy dips.
- Recovery modalities: light mobility work daily; shoulder and thoracic mobility daily; light cardio or walking on rest days.

Optional conditioning and lifestyle components
- Light cardio on rest days: 20–30 minutes of easy cycling, brisk walk, or gentle swimming to support appetite and recovery.
- Mobility routines: 5–10 minutes focusing on hip hinge, ankle, thoracic spine, and shoulder health to support lifts.
- Stress management: breathing exercises or mindfulness 5–10 minutes daily to support recovery.

Progression criteria
- Week 1 -> Week 2: If form is clean, sleep and appetite are stable, and fatigue is manageable, proceed with the Week 2 increases. If any regression in form or persistent fatigue occurs, hold at Week 1 intensity for another week or substitute lighter variants (e.g., swap barbell squats for goblet squats, reduce sets by 1–2 on each exercise).
- Week 2 -> Week 3: Increase main lifts by 2.5–5% or add 1–2 reps on 1–2 sets where appropriate, ensuring RPE remains 7–8 and form is solid. If technical form degrades or fatigue is excessive, hold Week 3 intensity until readiness improves.

Return-to-baseline target
- By the end of Week 3, the client should be showing improved energy, appetite, and lifting tolerance, with weights moving toward pre-illness baselines on the main lifts (bench close to 100 kg, squat approaching ~130–140 kg, deadlift ~160–165 kg depending on recovery and technique). The emphasis remains on safe progression rather than maximal loading.

Deliverable summary
- 3-week reconditioning block
- 4 training days per week; upper/lower body split with a balance of big lifts and accessory work
- Progressive load increases aligned with readiness
- Emphasis on technique, RPE targets, recovery, nutrition, and sleep
- Clear guidance to back off if symptoms reappear or fatigue spikes

If you want, I can tailor specifics to your client’s current weight, available equipment (e.g., if you have a power rack, bench brands, or particular machines), or any injury considerations.

Short answer: starting at pre-illness loads after a 3-week layoff and 4 kg weight drop is not prudent for Week 1. It walks the line between a smart reintroduction and a risk of overreaching, relapse, or extended fatigue.

Here’s how I’d evaluate and respond, with a plan if you still want to push toward a faster return.

Key considerations

- Illness impact and fatigue status
  - Even mild flu can dampen neuromuscular efficiency, glycogen stores, and immune function. Three weeks off compounds the regression in rate of force development.
  - A 4 kg weight loss likely reflects reduced intake, possible dehydration, and depleted substrates. Returning to baseline loads immediately ignores these recovery deficits.

- Readiness signals
  - Feeling fine today is a positive acute signal, but readiness must be evaluated across multiple days and sessions (sleep quality, appetite, HRV/resting HR, soreness, cough/respiratory effort, mood, digestion).
  - The plan should be flexible: if any red flags appear (fatigue crash after a set, prolonged soreness, elevated resting HR, poor sleep), back off immediately.

- Injury/overtraining risk
  - Returning to or exceeding 100% loads too quickly can provoke inflammation, prolonged DOMS, or reluctance to train later in the block.
  - The 3-week reconditioning block is designed to rebuild tolerance with controlled stimuli; skipping it increases risk of a relapse into illness or injury.

- Practicality and outcomes
  - The goal of Week 1 is to reestablish movement patterns, confidence, and baseline tolerances with relatively modest volumes, then ramp up safely in Weeks 2–3.
  - Moving straight to pre-illness loads would likely produce lower-quality reps, potential compensations, and could derail the progress timeline you laid out.

What I’d propose instead (compromise approach)

- Start with Week 1 loads but adjust dialing for readiness, not maximum loads.
  - Main lifts at the lower end of your Week 1 targets (bench 60–65 kg, squat 85 kg, deadlift 105–110 kg) with 3x5–3x6 schemes or 3x6 depending on lift.
  - Keep the same weekly structure (4 days) but use slightly lighter accessory work and longer rest if needed to preserve technique.
  - Treat the first week as “load acclimation” with an emphasis on technique, bracing, breathing, and tempo.

- Use RPE rather than pure percentage
  - Target RPE 6 on main sets, with room to back off if form trends downward.
  - If technique remains solid and the lifter reports stable fatigue, you can add a small progression in Week 2 (RPE 6–7).

- Monitor objective readiness markers daily
  - Morning resting HR, sleep duration/quality, appetite, and a simple fatigue questionnaire.
  - If any marker worsens by more than small margins for two consecutive days, pause progress, revert to Week 1 levels, and reassess.

- Optional: lighter alternative for Week 1
  - If he feels exceptionally fresh and you want to avoid stalling adaptation, you could implement Week 1 with a reduced volume approach: 2–3 sets per main lift instead of 3, keep reps controlled, and omit a couple of accessory movements to allow recovery.

A concrete plan if you still want to push near pre-illness loads

- Week 1 (modified, not full pre-illness load)
  - Bench: 3x5 at 60–65 kg or 65–70% of 1RM if you’ve reassessed true 1RM post-illness (keep RPE 6–6.5)
  - Squat: 3x4–5 at 85–95 kg (60–65% of 140 kg baseline) with RPE 6
  - Deadlift: 3x4 at 105–115 kg (60–70% of 170 kg) with RPE 6
  - Accessory work and cardio as planned, but with conservative volumes (e.g., shaving 1–2 sets from select exercises)
  - Rest: 2–3 minutes for all main lifts; 1–2 minutes for accessories

- Week 2–3 follow the progressive scheme you outlined earlier, ramping volume and intensity based on readiness.

What I’d recommend you do next

- If you want to attempt a slightly accelerated schedule, implement Week 1 with the conservative main lift targets as above, then re-evaluate after Week 1 with objective feedback (sleep, appetite, HR, soreness). If all looks good, proceed to Week 2 with the planned progression.
- If any red flags appear (significant fatigue, persistent soreness, appetite drop, sleep disturbance), revert to the original Week 1 structure and don’t accelerate.

Bottom line: It’s reasonable to take a cautious approach rather than jumping straight to pre-illness loads. A short Week 1 with conservative loading nudges you toward readiness without risking a setback. Great question. Readiness for full-intensity work after a hiatus and illness is best judged by a combination of objective metrics, subjective feeling, and training response. Here’s a practical checklist you can use day-to-day and week-to-week to decide when to push to higher intensities.

Subjective readiness signals (daily checks)
- Energy and mood: stable or improved energy throughout the day; no persistent fatigue lingering after workouts.
- Appetite: returning to baseline appetite (not unusually suppressed or ravenous).
- Sleep: 7–9 hours with good quality; minimal awakenings.
- Soreness: manageable DOMS/awked muscle soreness that dissipates within 24–48 hours; no unusual joint pain or bone pain.
- Respiratory/Burn: no lingering cough, chest tightness, or dyspnea during light activity.
- Motivation and focus: positive training motivation and ability to concentrate during technique checks.

Objective readiness signals (quantitative checks)
- Resting heart rate (RHR): compare to established baseline. 
  - Normal: within 1–5 bpm of baseline on most days.
  - Warning: several days of RHR elevated by 5–8+ bpm suggests under-recovery.
- HRV (if available): stable or improving HRV; declining HRV over multiple days can indicate fatigue or stress overload.
- Performance tolerance in controlled sets:
  - Main lifts: you can complete planned near-maximal sets with same or better technique and no drastic form breakdown.
  - Tempo and bar speed: controlled but not visibly sluggish; you can maintain intended tempo (e.g., 2–0–2 or 3–0–2 cadence) and bar speed consistent with prior sessions.
- Technical competency: no recurring compensations (rounded back, excessive lumbar extension, knee valgus, loss of bracing, depth issues) when performing main lifts.
- Recovery markers: resting heart rate recovery after sets/back-to-back days is reasonable; you can recover within 24–48 hours.

Concrete readiness rubric (useful for weekly decision-making)
- Level 0: Not ready – symptoms present (fatigue, poor sleep, appetite loss, elevated RHR, mood dips). Do not increase intensity; maintain light work or de-load.
- Level 1: Partial readiness – you can tolerate light-to-moderate work; keep intensity limited to RPE 6–7 on main lifts, avoid pushing to technical failure.
- Level 2: Ready for cautious intensity – you can handle moderate intensity on main lifts (RPE 7–8) with clean technique; plan progressive overload in small steps (e.g., +2.5–5% or +1–2 reps) in the next micro-cycle.
- Level 3: Ready for high intensity – you can regularly perform near-maximal or near-baseline intensities (RPE 8–9) on main lifts with solid technique and good recovery signals.

Decision rules to progress or back off
- If 2–3 days in a row show Level 2 or Level 3 readiness without RHR drift, sleep issues, or appetite loss, you can progress to higher intensity in that block.
- If you notice any Level 0 or multiple Day-to-day Level 1 signals, pause progression, revert to previous week’s loads, and add extra recovery (deload micro-cycle, more cardio-only days, reduced volume).
- If HRV and RHR trend worsens over 3–5 days despite adequate sleep and nutrition, back off immediately and reassess overall stress (training load, life factors, sleep).

Practical weekly approach
- Week-to-week readiness check: At the end of each training week, review:
  - Are main lifts maintaining technique with at least 2–3 progressing sets vs the prior week?
  - Has RHR stayed within baseline margins or improved?
  - Is appetite and sleep back to baseline?
  - Any persistent soreness or fatigue beyond 48 hours?
- If yes to most, advance the main lifts modestly in the next week (e.g., +2.5–5% or +1–2 reps on sets where appropriate).
- If no, maintain Week n intensity for another week or revert to Week n-1 loads with an emphasis on technique, mobility, and recovery.

Signals specific to reconditioning after illness
- Ephemeral signals are common: slight fatigue spikes, mood dips, minor appetite fluctuations in Week 1–2. They typically normalize by Week 3 if nutrition, sleep, and stress are managed.
- Avoid chasing absolute weights until you’ve demonstrated consistent technique, stable energy, and completing sessions without unplanned soreness or fatigue.

Optional monitoring tools
- Simple daily checklist: sleep hours, energy, appetite, mood, soreness; note on a 1–5 scale.
- Quick performance tests (every 2–4 weeks): establish or re-establish current 1RM estimates or triple-rep max at submax loads to gauge true readiness.
- Objective metrics: track resting HR and optional HRV using a wearable app if available.

Bottom line
- Readiness for full intensity work is determined by a combination of: stable energy and sleep, appetite restoration, absence of persistent fatigue or respiratory symptoms, and the ability to perform main lifts with correct technique at controlled RPE with acceptable bar speed and recovery.
- Start with a conservative progression, then advance only when multiple readiness signals align positively. If any red flags appear, slow down or revert to safer loads and focus on recovery and technique.

Great idea. Introducing a formal 1RM test in the back half of Week 3 gives you objective baselines to reset the program. Here’s a practical, safe integration that respects the reconditioning timeline and minimizes risk.

Overview of plan
- Objective: obtain updated 1RM estimates for bench, squat, and deadlift, then re-baseline the next 12-week program from these values.
- Timing: Week 3, on a test day toward the end of the week (e.g., Day A for upper, Day B for lower, or a dedicated test day after light activation work). Ideally no more than one heavy testing session per day; separate tests by at least 48–72 hours if you’re testing multiple lifts in one day.
- Readiness criteria: only proceed with the 1RM attempts if the client has shown consistent readiness signals across the preceding two weeks (stable sleep, appetite, RHR within baseline range, no lingering symptoms, technically solid lifts).

Safety and prep considerations
- Warm-up protocol: start with 5–10 minutes light cardio, then mobility for shoulders, hips, and thoracic spine. Use an escalating warm-up specifically tailored to each lift.
- Submaximal ladder: use a progressive loading scheme to estimate 1RM without reaching true maxes. A common approach is:
  - Bench: work up to 5–6 singles at increasing loads (e.g., 60, 70, 80, 90% of prior estimated 1RM or current work sets) with 2–3 minutes rest, then attempt a single at a challenging weight and extrapolate an estimate.
  - Squat/Deadlift: similar ladder approach with careful attention to form and spinal neutral positions.
- RPE targets during test: keep attempts in the 8–9 range for the top attempts only; avoid grinding to failure. Use a conservative progression to avoid form breakdown.
- Recovery: ensure ample post-test nutrition, hydration, and sleep. Consider a lighter day after the test if performance is suboptimal or fatigue is elevated.

Proposed Week 3 structure with test day
- Day A – Upper body (bench emphasis) and readiness check
  - Warm-up as per plan
  - Bench press main line: 3 x 5 @ RPE 7–8, then attempt 1–2 singles approaching max with technique control
  - Record best successful max rep at a given load (or 1RM estimate via a rep-max calculation if you prefer)
  - Accessory work as per Week 3 plan, adjusted if you felt fatigued from testing

- Day B – Lower body (squat emphasis) and test
  - Warm-up
  - Back squat: 3–4 working sets building to a top single at ~90% of prior 1RM if technique holds
  - Attempt 1–2 singles for 1RM estimate, using bar speed and depth to judge acceptability
  - Follow with Romanian deadlift and lighter accessory work

- Day C – Upper body (pulling emphasis) – light to moderate
  - Since testing is on bench, keep Day C moderate to avoid overfatigue for a high-intensity test day
  - 3–4 sets of rowing/pulling with emphasis on form; no near-max attempts

- Day D – Lower body accessory and conditioning – light
  - Heavy testing day may leave residual fatigue; use this day for lighter squats or deadlift variants at reduced volume if needed
  - Finish with mobility work and light cardio

What to record and how to reset after the test
- Record actual 1RM or best single per lift, plus:
  - Warm-up weights, reps completed, and RPE for every attempt
  - Bar speed perception (if you have velocity tools) or coaching observations on technique and stability
  - Any deviations from ideal technique (depth, bar path, torso angle) and corrective notes
- Post-test plan
  - Allow 48–72 hours before resuming training with a full reset phase. Start the new block 1–2 weeks after the testing day with a de-load or reduced volume if needed.
  - For the next 3–4 weeks after the test, use revised 1RM-based working loads for main lifts, then stage into the standard 12-week progression you prefer.
  - Re-calculate estimated training maxes (TM or 1RM estimates) using the common formula: 1RM_est = 1RM_true if you got a true max, or use a 3–5RM extrapolation or Epley/Brzycki formulas for the next cycle.

Concrete example of test weight planning (illustrative)
- If Week 3 main lifts at the end look like:
  - Bench main sets at 60–65 kg for 3x5 with form solid
  - Squat main sets at 85–95 kg for 3–4 sets
  - Deadlift top set around 110–120 kg for 3–5 reps
- You might attempt:
  - Bench single at 70–75 kg, then 80 kg if form is clean
  - Squat single at 100–105 kg, then 110–115 kg if depth and brace hold
  - Deadlift single at 125–130 kg, then 140 kg if technique is solid
- Use a conservative maximum: only attempt 1RM if a previous attempt indicates a clear path to success with good form.

Communication and expectations
- Discuss with your client the purpose of the test: to re-baseline so future programming is precise, safe, and aligned with actual capacity.
- Emphasize tolerable risk: if at any point technique deteriorates or fatigue spikes, abort the attempt and revert to a controlled submaximal plan.

Here’s a concise, integrative summary of the 3-week reconditioning block, tying together loads, rest, and cardio progression. Use it as a quick reference for programming and client handoffs.

Overall structure
- Frequency: 4 training days per week (2 upper, 2 lower), plus optional light cardio on rest days or after sessions.
- Principles: conservative loads Week 1, modestly increasing Week 2, near-baseline but controlled loads Week 3 with a 1RM test toward the end.
- Readiness monitoring: RPE targets, sleep, appetite, resting HR (and optional HRV), soreness, and technique first.

Week 1 — Reintroduction and capacity restoration
- Main lifts (low-to-moderate load; RPE targets ~6)
  - Bench press: 3 × 6 @ 60–65 kg (about 60–65% of pre-illness 1RM)
  - Squat: 3 × 5 @ 84–91 kg (60–65% of 140 kg)
  - Deadlift: 3 × 4–5 @ 102–119 kg (60–70% of 170 kg)
- Accessory work: upper and lower body 3 × 8–12 per movement, tempo-focused, bracing emphasis
- Cardio: 2–3 sessions totaling ~20–40 minutes per week, zone 2
  - Optional: light cardio finisher after lifting (10–12 minutes)
- Rest and recovery
  - Rest between main sets: 2–3 minutes (longer for heavier sets)
  - Sleep target: 7–9 hours
  - Monitoring: daily check of energy, appetite, sleep; watch for excessive fatigue or soreness

Week 2 — Gradual load increase and volume up
- Main lifts (moderate load; RPE targets ~6–7 for most sets; some 7–8 as readiness allows)
  - Bench press: 4 × 5 @ 60–70% of pre-illness 1RM (adjust if needed based on Week 1 response)
  - Squat: 4 × 4 @ 60–65% of pre-illness 1RM
  - Deadlift: 3–4 × 4–5 @ ~60–70% of pre-illness 1RM
- Accessory work: maintain 3 × 6–8 to 3 × 10–12, ensure technique
- Cardio: increase to 20–25 minutes per session on lifting days; 1–2 additional easy sessions (10–20 minutes) if tolerated
- Rest and recovery
  - 2–3 minutes for main lifts; 1–2 minutes for accessories
  - Sleep 7–9 hours; monitor HR and appetite
  - Readiness check: if form is clean and fatigue is manageable, push Week 2 intensities; if not, hold or deload slightly

Week 3 — Near-baseline strength with a 1RM test window
- Main lifts (near baseline intensity; RPE targets ~7–8)
  - Bench press: 3 × 5 @ ~7–8 RPE; then 1–2 singles to estimate 1RM (test day structure)
  - Squat: 3–4 × 4–5 @ ~7–8 RPE; optional top single if technique holds
  - Deadlift: 3–4 × 4–5 @ ~7–8 RPE; optional top single if technique holds
- 1RM testing window (late Week 3)
  - Schedule on a dedicated test day or split across two days if needed
  - Use warm-up ladder, progressively heavier singles with strict technique
  - Record actual 1RM or best single per lift for resetting the program
- Cardio
  - Maintain 2–3 sessions, with one light run/walk day (if cardio earlier included) and one easy zone-2 workout per week
  - If returning to running, keep easy pace and gradually normalize to ~10k/week equivalent across the week
- Rest and recovery
  - Post-test deload window: allow 48–72 hours before resuming a new block
  - Sleep 7–9 hours; nutrition to support regeneration (protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day, caloric intake around maintenance + small surplus if weight recovery goals persist)

Return-to-programming after Week 3
- Use Week 3 1RM results to set new training maxes (TM) and re-baseline the next 12-week plan.
- Rebuild cycles: progressively overload from the new baselines with the same upper/lower split philosophy, adjusting volume and intensity per readiness signals.

Notes and customization
- If any red flags appear (persistent fatigue, sleep disruption, appetite loss, elevated resting heart rate, poor technique), revert to Week 1 targets for another cycle and reassess before advancing.
- If the client prefers more cardio or has a longer endurance background, you can slightly increase Week 1–2 cardio minutes while preserving strength quality.
- If a specific lift regresses or technique degrades, slow progression or replace that lift with a regression (e.g., goblet squat for back squat, DB floor press for bench) until readiness improves.

Here’s a concise, integrative summary of the 3-week reconditioning block, tying together loads, rest, and cardio progression. Use it as a quick reference for programming and client handoffs.

Overall structure
- Frequency: 4 training days per week (2 upper, 2 lower), plus optional light cardio on rest days or after sessions.
- Principles: conservative loads Week 1, modestly increasing Week 2, near-baseline but controlled loads Week 3 with a 1RM test toward the end.
- Readiness monitoring: RPE targets, sleep, appetite, resting HR (and optional HRV), soreness, and technique first.

Week 1 — Reintroduction and capacity restoration
- Main lifts (low-to-moderate load; RPE targets ~6)
  - Bench press: 3 × 6 @ 60–65 kg (about 60–65% of pre-illness 1RM)
  - Squat: 3 × 5 @ 84–91 kg (60–65% of 140 kg)
  - Deadlift: 3 × 4–5 @ 102–119 kg (60–70% of 170 kg)
- Accessory work: upper and lower body 3 × 8–12 per movement, tempo-focused, bracing emphasis
- Cardio: 2–3 sessions totaling ~20–40 minutes per week, zone 2
  - Optional: light cardio finisher after lifting (10–12 minutes)
- Rest and recovery
  - Rest between main sets: 2–3 minutes (longer for heavier sets)
  - Sleep target: 7–9 hours
  - Monitoring: daily check of energy, appetite, sleep; watch for excessive fatigue or soreness

Week 2 — Gradual load increase and volume up
- Main lifts (moderate load; RPE targets ~6–7 for most sets; some 7–8 as readiness allows)
  - Bench press: 4 × 5 @ 60–70% of pre-illness 1RM (adjust if needed based on Week 1 response)
  - Squat: 4 × 4 @ 60–65% of pre-illness 1RM
  - Deadlift: 3–4 × 4–5 @ ~60–70% of pre-illness 1RM
- Accessory work: maintain 3 × 6–8 to 3 × 10–12, ensure technique
- Cardio: increase to 20–25 minutes per session on lifting days; 1–2 additional easy sessions (10–20 minutes) if tolerated
- Rest and recovery
  - 2–3 minutes for main lifts; 1–2 minutes for accessories
  - Sleep 7–9 hours; monitor HR and appetite
  - Readiness check: if form is clean and fatigue is manageable, push Week 2 intensities; if not, hold or deload slightly

Week 3 — Near-baseline strength with a 1RM test window
- Main lifts (near baseline intensity; RPE targets ~7–8)
  - Bench press: 3 × 5 @ ~7–8 RPE; then 1–2 singles to estimate 1RM (test day structure)
  - Squat: 3–4 × 4–5 @ ~7–8 RPE; optional top single if technique holds
  - Deadlift: 3–4 × 4–5 @ ~7–8 RPE; optional top single if technique holds
- 1RM testing window (late Week 3)
  - Schedule on a dedicated test day or split across two days if needed
  - Use warm-up ladder, progressively heavier singles with strict technique
  - Record actual 1RM or best single per lift for resetting the program
- Cardio
  - Maintain 2–3 sessions, with one light run/walk day (if cardio earlier included) and one easy zone-2 workout per week
  - If returning to running, keep easy pace and gradually normalize to ~10k/week equivalent across the week
- Rest and recovery
  - Post-test deload window: allow 48–72 hours before resuming a new block
  - Sleep 7–9 hours; nutrition to support regeneration (protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day, caloric intake around maintenance + small surplus if weight recovery goals persist)

Return-to-programming after Week 3
- Use Week 3 1RM results to set new training maxes (TM) and re-baseline the next 12-week plan.
- Rebuild cycles: progressively overload from the new baselines with the same upper/lower split philosophy, adjusting volume and intensity per readiness signals.

Notes and customization
- If any red flags appear (persistent fatigue, sleep disruption, appetite loss, elevated resting heart rate, poor technique), revert to Week 1 targets for another cycle and reassess before advancing.
- If the client prefers more cardio or has a longer endurance background, you can slightly increase Week 1–2 cardio minutes while preserving strength quality.
- If a specific lift regresses or technique degrades, slow progression or replace that lift with a regression (e.g., goblet squat for back squat, DB floor press for bench) until readiness improves.
